title: Metacognitive Knowledge and Metacognitive Regulation in Self-Regulatory Learning Style, and in Its Effects on Performance Expectation and Subsequent Performance across Diverse School Subjects
extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students’ metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation relate to their self-regulatory learning styles, performance expectations, and actual school performance. The authors focus on whether different components of metacognition—declarative, procedural, conditional knowledge, and planning, monitoring, information management, and evaluation—are associated with students’ motivation and achievement across three school subjects: language, mathematics, and physical education.

The study sampled 243 fifth- and sixth-grade students from 20 state primary schools in Greece, along with 25 teachers who rated student performance. Students completed self-report questionnaires in the middle of the school year, including the Junior Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and the Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire, plus subject-specific performance expectation scales. Teachers provided term grades and ratings of student performance. The analyses were correlational/regression-based and did not test an intervention.

The findings suggest that students reported moderate metacognitive knowledge and regulation, with declarative knowledge and planning used most often and evaluation least often. Students showed a mixed self-regulatory profile, with identified regulation most prominent. Greater metacognition, especially metacognitive regulation, was associated with more adaptive regulatory styles and better performance expectations, but effects varied by subject. External regulation consistently predicted poorer performance, while performance expectations were the strongest positive predictor of achievement; metacognition contributed both directly and indirectly, especially in mathematics and language.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study with self-report measures and teacher-rated outcomes, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful associative evidence but does not meet stronger causal-inference criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest-to-moderate associations in general elementary-school populations, with several statistically significant predictors and some meaningful variance explained. However, because the study is correlational and not an intervention test, the practical impact is unclear and should be considered modest.

finding.finding_summary: In a correlational study of 243 Greek 5th- and 6th-grade students, metacognition and self-regulatory style were associated with motivational beliefs and achievement. Higher metacognition, especially metacognitive regulation, predicted more self-determined regulation styles, and external regulation negatively predicted performance across subjects. Performance expectations were positively related to later performance, with the strongest models in mathematics (R2=0.29) and language (R2=0.22), but weaker in physical education (R2=0.095).
finding.measure: Self-regulation questionnaire, performance expectations, and teacher/school-record performance ratings across language, mathematics, and physical education
finding.effect_size: R2=0.22; R2=0.29; R2=0.095; beta values reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily examines metacognition and self-regulated learning. Students reported moderate metacognitive knowledge (declarative M=4.27, procedural M=3.20, conditional M=4.09) and metacognitive regulation (planning M=4.06, monitoring M=3.82, information management M=3.72, evaluation M=3.51), with planning the most used component and evaluation the least used. Metacognitive regulation significantly predicted identified regulation (R2=0.22) and intrinsic motivation (R2=0.13), while monitoring negatively predicted external regulation (beta=-0.23).
finding.measure: Junior Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.67 years; SDs for scale means reported in text

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics outcomes showed positive associations with metacognition, self-regulation, and performance expectations, but with important null/negative components. In the performance model, the combined predictors explained 29% of variance (R2=0.29), with performance expectations the strongest positive predictor (beta=0.40) and external regulation a negative predictor (beta=-0.25); procedural knowledge also contributed positively (beta=0.14).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in mathematics; performance expectations in mathematics

finding.finding_summary: In physical education, the combined predictors explained only a small share of performance variance (R2=0.095), and metacognition/self-regulation had mostly indirect or non-significant effects. Performance expectations positively predicted performance (b=0.18), while external regulation was a negative contributor (b=-15), and identified regulation was the only positive predictor of expectations (beta=0.25).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in physical education; performance expectations in physical education

finding.finding_summary: Language outcomes were positively associated with metacognition, self-regulation, and performance expectations, but external regulation showed a negative association with school performance. The predictors explained 22% of variance in language performance (R2=0.22); performance expectations was the strongest positive predictor (beta=0.29), followed by introjected regulation (beta=0.24) and declarative knowledge (beta=0.13), whereas external regulation was negative (beta=-0.24).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in language; performance expectations in language
